To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the failure of immune effectors mechanisms to control HIV-1 infection is a consequence of the inability to induce cellular immune responses to the HIV-1 envelope protein.

1) the proliferative response of PBMC to HIV‐1 Env is restricted in the majority of HIV‐inflicted subjects; 2) therapeutic vaccination with rgp120/160 restores the proliferative response; 3) IL‐7, and to a lesser degree, IL‐12, differentially modulate proliferative responses to gp160; and 4) the effect of IL7 is greatest in subjects who have been previously exposed to HIV‐1, while IL‐12

1) the proliferative response of PBMC to gp160 was restricted, and 2) the restriction could be overcome by therapeutic vaccination with rgp160 or rgp120, 3) IL‐7 augmented responses in individuals with pre‐existing gp160‐specific T cells, and 4) IL‐12 augmented responses in individuals without pre‐existing gp120‐specific T cells
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a vaccine to prevent infection with the human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV‐1) by the mucosal route.
the immunology of HIV infection and the development of vaccines for HIV infection.
the mechanisms of the host immune responses to HIV infection and with the development of novel therapeutic strategies to improve the efficacy of these responses.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
IL‐7 is a more effective cytokine than IL‐12 for augmenting cellular proliferative responses in HIV‐1‐infected individuals.

(a) HIV‐1 infection is associated with a restricted proliferative response to Env; (b) this restriction is reversed by vaccination with rgp160 and/or gp120; (c) IL‐7 and/or IL‐12 can augment the proliferative response of PBMC to Env, but with different effects; (d) IL‐7 is most active in individuals who have previously been primed by antigen exposure, while the effect IL‐12 is predominantly seen in unprimed,
the use of IL‐7 or the combination of IL‐7 and gp120 or gp160 may be a useful strategy for enhancing cellular responses to HIV‐infected cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the restricted cellular immune responses observed in the majority of HIV‐1‐infected patients are not due to the loss of T cell function.
we found that the majority of HIV‐infaced individuals have restricted proliferative responses against the HIV‐1 envelope (Env), gp 160, in vitro.
IL‐7 and/or IL‐12 can be used to augment the cellular proliferative response to Env.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have shown that IL‐7 and/or IL‐12 may have a beneficial effect on the ability of the immune system to mount a response to a HIV‐1 vaccine.
IL‐7, and possibly IL‐12, can be used to boost the cellular immune response to HIV‐specific antigens in the setting of vaccination.
the cytokines IL‐7 and/or IL‐12 can be used to expand the immune response to HIV‐specific proteins.
